vignette:
Khalil's Vigil

Khalil Mansour was fifty-five years old when a man he had hired to help with seasonal work turned on him in the barn. It was late afternoon in October, the light already dimming through the gaps in the wooden slats, when the worker—someone Khalil had known casually for two seasons—suddenly produced a knife and demanded money. Khalil, a sturdy man accustomed to the physical demands of his farm in rural Pennsylvania, had tried to reason with him first. When that failed, he resisted. The man was younger, faster. Khalil remembered the initial shock of the blade, the burning sensation, but what came after fragmented into pieces that would not cohere. He remembered the smell of his own sweat, acrid and unfamiliar, mixing with the metallic scent of blood and dust. He remembered the man's face, but not clearly—it kept shifting in his mind's eye, sometimes angry, sometimes blank. He remembered falling, his palms scraping concrete, but he could not quite place where the concrete was or how he had gotten there. The ambulance arrived. Stitches. The police. But the sequence felt borrowed from someone else's story, something he had read rather than lived.

The assault had left him with physical scars that healed reasonably well. The psychological aftermath was slower to surface. For the first few weeks, Khalil had thrown himself into work with an intensity that alarmed his wife, Yasmine. He would be in the fields before dawn and would not come inside until dark, pushing through tasks that did not need pushing, reorganizing the equipment shed for the third time, scrubbing the barn floor until his hands bled. Yasmine understood this as a coping mechanism—he was a man who had always solved problems through labor—but she also noticed that he would not speak about what had happened. When she asked, he would start to explain and then lose the thread of his own narrative. "He came in, and I—" he would begin, then pause, his jaw tightening, unable to continue. It was as though the memory belonged to someone else entirely, something he had witnessed rather than endured.

By the following October, the anniversary month, Khalil became noticeably withdrawn. He had begun to avoid the barn in the weeks leading up to the date, delegating tasks to his son-in-law, something he had never done before. The avoidance extended further: he would not drive past the intersection where the police car had first turned onto his property; he would not listen to the news; he had stopped attending the mosque's Friday gatherings, claiming he was too tired. What Yasmine did not know was that Khalil was ruminating constantly about the assailant—where he was now, whether he had been released from prison, what Khalil would do if he saw him again. He had fantasies of confrontation, of evening the score, scenarios that played out in his head as he lay awake at night. These thoughts were shameful to him; they contradicted his faith and his nature, yet he could not stop them.

The real crisis came when Khalil's heart began to race unpredictably. A sudden acceleration would seize him—his pulse pounding in his ears, his chest tight—and he would become convinced that something terrible was about to happen. His own body had become a trigger. The sensation of his heart racing reminded him of the assault, though he could not articulate why or how. When his neighbor stopped by to discuss crop rotation and stood too close, Khalil felt his pulse spike. When a new hand was hired to help with the harvest, Khalil watched him with an intensity that bordered on paranoia, reading threat into casual movements, into the way the man wiped sweat from his brow.

It was Yasmine who finally insisted he see someone. She had found him in the barn at three in the morning, sitting alone in the dark, and when she asked what he was doing, he could not answer. He had come to believe that something was fundamentally broken in him, that the man who had attacked him had left him permanently fractured. When his family doctor referred him to a therapist, Khalil agreed, though he carried deep doubt that talking would help him reassemble a memory that felt as though it had never truly been his own.
